title: SRD coverage: undead template constructions, pre-materialized
summary: Issue #43's decision is to ship the D&D templates as concrete creatures filling the same niche the templates serve, so a GM reaches for a Skeleton or a Lich the way the source books intend, without applying anything. These nine are the undead half of that: the animated dead built from the Skeleton and Zombie identities including the specific constructions the SRD prints beside them, and the four named undead the templates culminate in. Every one buys its unlife from published parts — Unliving or Diffuse injury tolerance, Unaging, immunity to metabolic hazards, and a mind either too empty to seize or too willful — and, as with the constructs, FP is stated explicitly because nothing here has a metabolism to tire. Edge mechanics no published trait prices, like a rot that outruns healing or a curse that travels in a wound, are carried in stat notes and priced through the affliction terms on the attacks that deliver them.

monsters.name: Skeleton
monsters.lair: Wherever it fell or was posted: a barrow passage, a crypt door, the bottom rank of somebody's cheap army.

attacks.name: Notched Blade
attacks.notes: Whatever weapon it was buried or posted with, swung with no fear of the answer.

attacks.name: Claw
attacks.notes: Finger bones driven like a handful of pegs.

monsters.description: Bones with the orders still in them. It does not tire, it does not flinch, and a blade between its ribs finds nothing there to matter. Crushing weapons end it fastest, because dry bone breaks in a way flesh does not.
notes: Brittle: any major wound shatters structure. Impaling and piercing weapons find nothing worth finding, so take the injury tolerance literally.
provenanceNotes: A human frame stripped to bone, which is the SM 0 row at about 20 lb.
FP is stated rather than derived: nothing here has a metabolism to tire.

monsters.name: Minotaur Skeleton
monsters.lair: A maze it no longer needs to understand to patrol.

attacks.name: Gore
attacks.notes: The horns kept their points when everything else went.

attacks.name: Greataxe
attacks.notes: Swung from the shoulder joints with no muscle to slow it down between blows.

monsters.description: A bull-horned frame two heads taller than a man, still walking its maze. The charge is what kills people. It does not slow into the turn, having nothing left that can pull a muscle.
provenanceNotes: The living creature's mass drops to bone; SM +1 for the frame's height.

monsters.name: Warhorse Skeleton
monsters.lair: A stable nobody mucks out, or the barrow of whoever it was buried to carry.

attacks.name: Hooves
attacks.notes: A kick with the full frame behind it and no instinct for self-preservation holding it back.

monsters.description: A rider's mount reduced to its running gear. It carries whatever it is told to carry, at a gallop it never breaks, and it does not shy — fear needed parts it no longer has.
provenanceNotes: Still a two-hex quadruped; the ground speed of the living animal is kept with a level of Enhanced Move.
It accepts any rider and no rider; a skeleton mount is tack, not a companion animal.

monsters.name: Zombie
monsters.lair: Graveyard mud, plague pits, the shallow end of a necromancer's budget.

attacks.name: Slam
attacks.notes: A dead weight of an arm brought down like a falling beam, and then the grip that follows it.

monsters.description: The recently dead, put back to work. One zombie is a chore for anybody with a weapon and room to move. There is never one. They come in the numbers they were buried in, they do not stop for wounds that should drop them, and whichever doorway is being held is the only direction they need.
provenanceNotes: Hard to Kill 3 carries the source identity's refusal to fall to what ought to be a finishing blow; a zombie that checks out at 0 HP frequently gets back up.
Slow on purpose: DX below human and no move advantages. Its threat is arithmetic, not skill, and the appearing number is the real stat line.

monsters.name: Ogre Zombie
monsters.lair: Wherever its maker needed a door held or a gate broken.

attacks.name: Club
attacks.notes: A tree trunk swung on a dead shoulder; the follow-through does not care what it hits.

monsters.description: An ogre's frame with an ogre's reach and none of the ogre's interest in surviving. It is a siege tool that walks. Pointed at a shield wall or a door, it keeps hitting until one of the two is gone.
provenanceNotes: The living ogre's ST is kept; the sluggishness of the corpse shows up as reduced DX instead, which is what the source identity describes.

monsters.name: Ghost
monsters.lair: The place it cannot leave: the room it died in, the road it died on, the person it died for.

attacks.name: Withering Touch
attacks.notes: A hand through the chest, and the years it takes with it. Resist with HT or age visibly around the wound; armor is no answer to something that ignores the body's outside.

attacks.name: Horrifying Visage
attacks.notes: The face it wears when it stops pretending to be what it was. A Fright Check at penalty; those who fail are staggered by terror, and the young can be aged by it.

monsters.description: Somebody still here. It drifts through the walls of the place that holds it, and the cold spot in the room is the only warning before a hand comes out of the stonework. Killing it again buys a few days. Whatever holds it here has to be dealt with for anything more.
notes: Whatever binds it to the site is not on the stat block. Settle that, or it comes back.
provenanceNotes: Insubstantiality is bought with Affect Substantial: the touch works on the living, and walls, armor and grapples do not work on it. Weapons need magic or the spirit's own terms to bite; Diffuse injury tolerance carries that.
Massless and hovering; movement is flight at a walking pace.

monsters.name: Vampire
monsters.lair: A defended household with money, staff who do not ask, and a windowless room nobody mentions.

attacks.name: Bite
attacks.notes: Delivered to a grappled or willing victim. The wound is small; the draining is not, and a victim held through it loses blood by the round.

attacks.name: Slam
attacks.notes: Strength far past what the frame suggests.

attacks.name: Dominating Gaze
attacks.notes: Meet its eyes and resist with Will, or obey and remember it afterwards as a decision freely made. It prefers this to violence; violence is noisy.

monsters.description: A predator that owns property. It passes for a living aristocrat as long as it feeds carefully, and the household around it exists to keep the feeding careful. Sunlight burns it and it knows every hour of the almanac, so the fight on offer is the one it prepared: at night, indoors, on its ground.
notes: Sunlight does 1d per minute of exposure. Folklore's other bans — thresholds, running water, the stake — vary by telling and are the GM's to rule.
Wounds close on their own, which does not make it unkillable. Fire, beheading and daylight are the traditional ends and nothing here rules them out.
provenanceNotes: Fresh blood is a Restricted Diet, not an option: a vampire that will not feed weakens until it must.

monsters.name: Lich
monsters.lair: A tower, tomb or buried library arranged for the convenience of one scholar and the death of visitors, with its true treasure hidden somewhere else entirely.

attacks.name: Paralyzing Touch
attacks.notes: A hand like winter through the armor's gaps. Resist with HT or the body simply stops answering, and the lich walks past to the one it actually came for.

attacks.name: Deathly Bolt
attacks.notes: Stated as literal dice: the bolt is a property of the lich's art, not its arm. It costs the creature to cast, and a lich in its own lair has cheaper ways to open.

attacks.name: Frightening Gaze
attacks.notes: The full attention of something that outlived everyone's grandparents and expects to outlive their grandchildren. Fright Check at penalty; it uses this on the brave first.

monsters.description: A wizard who solved dying and went back to work. Everything about the encounter was settled before the party arrived — the approach, the ambush, which of them it wants alive to question. Destroying the body is an inconvenience. The vessel holding its life is somewhere else, and finding that is the real adventure.
notes: The stat block is the body in the room. The phylactery is not on it, and how the lich comes back is the GM's to decide.
provenanceNotes: The casting identity is carried by Magery 3 and the fatigue-costed attacks; a full spell list belongs to a character sheet, not a bestiary record, and the three attacks price what the rating can see of it.
Perception runs a point behind its towering IQ — centuries of reading by candlelight.

monsters.name: Mummy Lord
monsters.lair: The tomb complex it was interred to rule, with its organs in jars in a chamber it defends above its own body.

attacks.name: Rotting Fist
attacks.notes: The blow lands like a club, and what it leaves behind is worse: resist with HT or take the rot, a curse under the skin. Wounds will not close and healing arts fail until the curse itself is lifted.

attacks.name: Dreadful Glare
attacks.notes: The tomb's own verdict on trespass. Fright Check at penalty; a badly failed roll leaves the victim paralyzed by dread as it closes.

monsters.description: The buried king still holding court. Wrapped, preserved and furious, it runs its tomb like a garrison: it knows every trap and every shortcut, its priest-craft is intact, and its fist carries a rot that turns a survivable wound into a slow sentence. It will not pursue past its borders, and it has never needed to.
notes: The rot is a curse rather than a wound. It cannot be healed until the curse is lifted, and it does not wear off with rest.
provenanceNotes: Priestly magic is carried the same way the lich's wizardry is: Magery plus fatigue-costed attacks, with the full liturgy left to prose.
Burning was the old answer and remains a good one; nothing here prices it away.
